name: Honey and beetroot lip remedies

lead: People use beetroot juice as a natural pink or red lip tint and honey to leave lips softer and moisturized.

Beetroot's red color comes from betanin, a pigment used commercially as a red food colorant, so the stain shows on the lips right away. Honey has antibacterial activity in laboratory settings and preliminary evidence suggests faster healing of partial-thickness burns, but those findings concern wound care rather than lips. No published study of either for lip appearance was identified.

paras: Beetroot juice or a slice is dabbed onto the lips for a temporary tint, and honey is applied as a mask or balm and left on for a while before wiping off. The color fades with eating, drinking and washing.
Honey and beet products can cause allergic reactions in some people, and honey is not recommended for infants under one year when eaten. Beetroot can stain clothes and skin.

angle.text: Folk-remedy users apply beetroot juice for a natural pink tint and honey for softness. Beetroot's pigment stains the lips visibly and temporarily, while honey is used as a moisturizing coat. No lip studies exist for either.

lead: Honey and beetroot lip remedies are home practices for softer, rosier-looking lips: honey is applied for moisture and smoothness, and beetroot juice is dabbed on as a temporary pink-to-red tint. Home-beauty guides commonly combine them, mixing beet juice with honey and a fat such as coconut oil into a homemade tinted balm.

Beetroot owes its red colour to betanin, a betalain pigment extracted from beet juice and used commercially as a red food colourant, listed as E162. [1][2] Honey is a long-standing folk treatment for burns and skin injuries; it has antibacterial activity in laboratory settings and preliminary evidence of faster healing of partial-thickness burns, though these findings concern wound care and not lip colour. [3]

For looks, the payoff is plain: lips that look smoother and carry a natural-looking tint without lipstick. The colour is temporary, as betanin stains skin and washes off, and no published study of either substance for lip appearance was identified.

paras: Honey is a long-standing folk treatment for burns and skin injuries. Evidence for most wound uses is low quality, and the FDA has approved several medical-grade honey products for minor wounds and burns. [3] Honey is used on lips as a natural humectant in home recipes, in the same role that occlusive waxes and petrolatum play in commercial lip balms, which seal in moisture and protect thin lip skin from dry air and wind. [4]

Betanin is the red pigment in beetroot and is used in foods such as sauces, desserts and candy. [1] Its colour depends on pH, appearing bluish-red around pH 4 to 5 and shifting toward blue-violet as pH rises, and it degrades with light, heat and oxygen. [2] Wikipedia reports no safety concerns for betanin as a food additive and no link to clinical food allergy when used as a colourant, while a European Food Safety Authority panel found toxicity data too limited for conclusive evaluation. [2] The betanin article does not mention cosmetic uses. Eating beetroot can turn urine or stool reddish, which is harmless. [1]

Lips have thin tissue and no sweat glands, so they dry and chap easily. [5] Natural lip colour depends on blood visible through thin tissue and on melanin content. [5] Commercial lip balms combine waxes such as beeswax with ingredients such as petrolatum and may include colourants or sunscreen; some experts say fragrance in flavoured balms can irritate lip skin. [4]
